full_judgment:
4. The defendant Nuruddin died during the pendency of the suit and his heirs contested the same by filing a written statement. Upon denying the plaintiffs allegation, they asserted that the heirs of Fazar Ali first gave verbal lease to Nuruddin in the year 1936, accepted nazar and rents and placed him into possession of 1.61 acres out of the disputed land. Thereafter, the heirs of Fazar Ali, i.e. wife Bakumjan for hereself and on behalf of some of her minor children granted registered patta dated 29.6.38 and dakhilas in vavour of Nuruddin. He was in possession of 1.60 acres on payment of rent and he got corrected the record of right under Section 50 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Plaintiffs vendor Abdul Latif raised objection there but it was rejected. Plaintiffs vendor earlier instituted a suit, O.S. 235 of 1957, against Nuruddin for declaration of his title to the suit land which was dismissed on 2.7.1959. 

 18. It has been noticed by the Courts below and we have also seen that so far as documentary evidence is concerned relationg to payment of rent, record of right etc. the case of both the parties seem to stand at par. One of the grievances made by the learned Advocate for the appellants, however, is that the defendants documents, namely, Ext. B. C, D, E, G and H series were not at all considered by the learned Judge of the High Court Division. That this grievance has substance cannot be denied inasmuch as no reference is to be found to the said documents in the impugned judgment of the High Court Division. It appears that of the defendants' documents, the learned Judge of the High Court Division only considered Ext. A, certified copy of the patta dated 29.6.38 and observed, inter alia, that the same was completely demolished by the notice of the auction-purchaser under Section 167 of the B.T. Act. In view of the relevant provision of law referred to above, it is hardly necessary to point out that the notice under Section 167 B.T. Act was merely an exercise in futility. The documents and papers relating to auction sale and delivery of possession could hardly be of any help to the plaintiff for proving his possession. In the same manner, the P.S. Khatian, the dakhilas, although evidence of possession could hardly advance his case of actual possession of the suit land for the simple reason that the defendants had as much khatian and dakhilas in their names as were sufficient to match those of the plaintiffs. Among the large number of documents filed by the defendants showing mutation and payment of rent by them, reference may be made to Ext. C(2) which is a copy of the order sheet of Misc. Case No. 344 of 1964 under Section 50 of the Act. It appears that at the instance of Nuruddin, predecessor of the defendants the Revenue Officer ordered that 8 annas of Plot No. 2110 (i.e. 1.61 acres) be transferred to his Khatian No. 1215. Ext.C(3), E, E(1) F consistently support the defendant's case in respect of their share claimed out of the suit land. Dakhilas Ext. B series and H series are there in support of the defendants' case. However, we do not think that such documents proved on either side were such upon which actual possession could be decided. The plaintiff was at a disadvantage with his documents relating to his title for the reasons already stated. It was incumbent upon him to prove actual possession, by adducing oral evidence sufficient enough to carry conviction firstly, by his vendor Abdul Latif and then by himself. It will be seen that in order to prove possession plaintiff only examined himself as P.W.1 and his brother-in-law Badi Ahmed, P.W.2 and nobody else, Defendants on their part also examined two witnesses. In the facts and circumstances of the case noticed above it must be said that the evidence adduced by the plaintiff was not only meagre but wholly unconvincing for the purpose of proving actual possession in the suit land. Indeed there was no independent and reiable evidence on the side of the plaintiff to support his case of possession.
